reviews.title: Expensive, Underwhelming, and a Terrible First Experience - Stay Away!
reviews.text:
I subscribed to Runway Pro for $35/month, expecting a professional AI video platform that would support creative experimentation. Instead, two mediocre 12-second videos consumed nearly 75% of my entire monthly credit allowance.

That’s approximately 24 seconds of video for most of a $35 subscription.

The worst part? Runway’s own AI Agent selected expensive 1080p generation settings without clearly explaining the credit costs beforehand. When I questioned this, the Agent acknowledged that it should have warned me.

And the results weren’t even impressive. I was animating existing experimental artwork, and frankly, I’ve achieved better-looking results using Midjourney and Google’s Flow. Nothing about these videos justified the extraordinary credit consumption.

Customer support was equally disappointing. Rather than meaningfully addressing the experience or offering a credit adjustment, they directed me to Apple for a refund and eventually closed the conversation with “This is our final word here.”

I understand that Apple handles App Store refunds. That doesn’t explain why Runway couldn’t meaningfully address the credit consumption or offer some goodwill to a brand-new customer.

I’ve used other AI creative platforms, including Luma, where affordable draft generations made experimentation practical. Runway’s pricing and credit consumption, at least through this initial Agent workflow, made that kind of iteration financially unrealistic.

reviews.title: Inconsistent Results Leads to High Cost for Customers
reviews.text:
I wanted to love Runway because the quality of the individual images and videos can be outstanding. Unfortunately, the biggest weakness is consistency.

If you’re creating standalone clips, it’s impressive. But if you’re trying to produce a cinematic project with multiple connected scenes, the experience becomes frustrating and expensive.

In my experience, getting one usable image or video often takes five or six generations, and sometimes even more. Even after spending those credits, there’s still no guarantee the result will actually follow the prompt or preserve the reference images. Too often, one issue gets fixed while another is introduced.

The AI repeatedly changes things that are explicitly locked in the prompt, including character identity, apparent age, facial structure, objects, notebook continuity, sky, lighting, and scene details. Even when using reference images and very specific instructions, it often regenerates elements that were supposed to remain untouched.

The result is spending credits over and over just to repair mistakes introduced by the AI itself. A five-second correction can lead to another correction, then another, until you’ve spent far more credits than expected just trying to maintain continuity.

reviews.title: It’s ok, but not worth it.
reviews.text:
Truthfully, it’s clunky to use, images from my library don’t upload, or I can’t use them as base images because of some unknown bug that just doesn’t let me select new photos. Also, it’s just not worth your money. The videos it generates are decent at best, but if you’re a creator and it doesn’t get your content right, you just wasted a ton of credits for nothing. To be fair to Runway, the whole “credits” to utilize the models are a flawed business model entirely, for the simple reason that if you need to regenerate something, you’re essentially losing money by wasting credits on something it should have gotten right the first time. 

Also, if I’m paying you a subscription fee, maybe consider uncapping or at least expanding how many characters I’m allowed to type into any given model, especially when I need to waste words putting guardrails up that your models will still ignore. 

Tl;dr - not worth it unless you don’t care about your money spent regenerating videos over and over to get it right

reviews.title: Refund policy says “close to unused” — support denies anyway
reviews.text:
Bought a plan, realized quickly it wasn’t usable for my needs, and canceled within ~5 hours. During that short window I used credits only to troubleshoot because outputs were inaccurate/unusable — I wasn’t “using the service” in any meaningful way, I was testing whether it worked.

Runway’s own refund article says you can request a full refund within 30 days as long as the plan is “unused, or close to unused.” I requested a refund under that policy and was denied twice with the same brush-off response focusing on “credits used,” without explaining what “close to unused” means or why a few hours of troubleshooting disqualifies a refund.

Support rep only signs as “John,” won’t provide a supervisor review, and won’t give a clear, policy-based explanation — just canned denial.

If you value transparent billing and a refund policy that’s actually honored, be careful before subscribing.

reviews.title: Credits disappear, faster than results appear.
reviews.text:
Runway is extremely frustrating and poorly explained. The platform charges credits for image generations without clearly warning you upfront, and the credit system feels intentionally vague. You’re given a very small number of credits to start, and they disappear incredibly fast—often without producing usable results.

What makes it worse is that failed generations still consume credits. Half the time, a generation errors out or fails to produce anything meaningful, yet your credits are gone anyway. There’s no refund, no retry, and no transparency about why it failed.

For a paid AI platform, this is unacceptable. Between unclear credit usage, constant failures, and barely enough credits to experiment or learn the tool, it feels more like a trap than a creative platform. I would not recommend this to creators unless you’re prepared to burn money just to figure out how it works.

reviews.title: Scam
reviews.text:
I’m an educator who downloaded Runway expecting a reasonable learning experience. Within 15 minutes, my $15 monthly credits were completely gone — not from producing a finished video, but from simply trying to understand how the app works.

There is no protected learning or sandbox mode, no clear warning that experimentation will rapidly consume paid credits, and no transparency about how quickly costs escalate while learning.

This tool may be appropriate for professional studios or agencies billing clients, but for teachers, educators, or individual creators, the pricing model feels punitive and unethical. You pay real money to make basic mistakes that any new user will inevitably make.
